item.title: How to Raise a Confident, Independent Child
item.description:
Confidence

How to Raise a Confident, Independent Child

Children build real confidence through real decisions, not through praise alone.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Economic uncertainty shapes parenting choices—often without anyone in the family naming it directly.
  • Asking the question you'd normally answer yourself is one of the most effective ways to build autonomy.
  • Confidence built through real experience holds differently than confidence built through praise alone.

My daughter Carys runs a small pet-sitting business. One of her clients has a house that's been under renovation for longer than anyone in the neighborhood can remember. Out back there's a shed. That's where the cat lives. The owner was going to visit their daughter for a few days and didn't have anyone else to ask.

Carys said yes and charged less than her usual rate. She told me she figured the owner probably didn't have anyone else who'd take the job for what they could pay.

She's 10.

Why This Matters Now

The pressure to set children up for financial security has never felt more urgent. Trade school enrollment at public two-year schools grew almost 20 percent between 2020 and 2025. A four-year private college degree now runs close to two hundred thousand dollars, roughly double what it cost three decades ago. In one recent survey, 71 percent of Gen Z respondents said vocational school carries more stigma than college, while only 7 percent of their parents said they'd prefer their kid go the trade route.

Kids are more open to different paths than their parents are. And when economic uncertainty moves into a house, parents tend to respond in one of two ways.

One instinct watches for whether a child will be able to stand on their own two feet: steady income, safety, a way to pay rent without help. The other instinct watches for who this child is becoming, and whether the world is a little better because they're in it. Most parents hold some of both. The two don't always point the same direction.

The Third Option

There's a version of parenting where you hand your child a plan and expect them to follow it. There's another where you step back completely and hope things work out. Neither is really about your child. One is about the plan you had in mind. The other is about how uncomfortable it is to watch them struggle.

There's a third option: staying fully in the role of parent, but doing it differently. Guiding instead of directing. It's the difference between handing your child the answer and asking the question that helps them find it themselves. I've been exploring this in more depth on the Your Parenting Mojo podcast, but here's what it looks like in practice.

1. Ask, don’t build.

When Carys started taking on clients, she had a hard time keeping track of details like what each pet eats, where the key is hidden, and the alarm code. I could have built her a system and handed it to her. Instead, I asked her what would help her remember it all. She'd seen a pet sitter online use an intake form, so she built one. I helped her think through which questions to include. She designed it herself, and she still uses it.

article continues after advertisement

If you're wondering how to give your child more autonomy: Ask the question you'd normally answer yourself, and let them figure it out.

2. Let mistakes play out.

The first time Carys sat for a neighbor's cat, she forgot her intake form and couldn't remember the alarm code. The alarm went off. The next visit, she brought the form but pressed the disarm button in the wrong order. The alarm went off again.

I could have told her from the start to bring the form every single time. It would have saved everyone a headache. Instead, she worked it out for herself—after two false alarms and an understandably rattled neighbor. The next time she sat for that family, she brought the form to every visit and nothing went wrong.

Confidence built through real experience holds differently than confidence built through praise. A child who solves a problem, including one they created, comes away knowing they can handle things. That knowledge doesn't come from being told they did well.

3. Let the decision be theirs.

When Carys set her prices, we talked about how different families have different amounts of money to work with. Without any prompting from me, she decided to offer a sliding scale and let each family choose what fit their situation.

That decision was hers. She made a real call about her own business and lived with what it meant.

Research on self-determination supports what that experience points to: Confidence is more likely to endure when children experience themselves as capable decision-makers, rather than simply being praised for doing what they're told. The goal is a child who develops the judgment to make good decisions on their own.

4. Step back on purpose.

The instinct to jump in and fix things is strong. Most parents notice a version of it—watching a child struggle with a system they could solve in 30 seconds, choose a path that looks nothing like what you expected, or make a pricing decision you might have made differently.

You can support a child's growing independence by staying close enough to help if it's needed, and letting the decision itself belong to them. That's a skill you build the same way your child builds confidence, by practicing it in situations where the stakes are real but not catastrophic.

article continues after advertisement

Final Thoughts

Carys didn't set a sliding scale because I told her to think about fairness. She did it because she looked at the situation in front of her and made a call. That's the thing you're actually building toward—a child who can figure out what the right answer is.

That takes longer than handing them a plan. It's also the only way it sticks.

item.title: What Exactly Is Positive Mental Health?
item.description:
Happiness

What Exactly Is Positive Mental Health?

The six core dimensions experts agree that make up positive mental health.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Experts from different cultures and disciplines identified six core dimensions of positive mental health.
  • The dimensions of positive mental health include meaning and purpose, self-acceptance, and connection.
  • Mental health is a multidimensional construct with overlapping components.

Mental health has become a central trope of the Zeitgeist. As with the recent collective interest in optimizing physical health and longevity, people want to know how to get happier.

Body and mind are intricately connected, of course, despite our tendency to treat them as two separate riches to safeguard. When it comes to tending our bodies, we are inundated with advice on what to eat, how to move, when to rest. If we are trying to get stronger, reach a number on a scale, or alter key blood values, there is some or other well-paved road that leads to our goals.

Source: vilkasss / Pixabay

But when it comes to our minds, things are less straightforward. To begin with, we don’t even have a comprehensive picture of the very thing we are trying to improve—a construct that goes by many names: flourishing, mental well-being, mental health, quality of life. Poignantly, the field of happiness is fraught with intricacies and ambiguities that create challenges as much for the happiness-seekers as for the researchers and policy-makers seeking to implement interventions.

A recent study set out to address the fragmentation that dominates in well-being research by creating a preliminary taxonomy of the dimensions that make up positive mental health. The study used the Delphi consensus method—a structured technique for tapping into collective intelligence. This method is used across various fields to reach a consensus among a panel of experts through multiple rounds of questionnaires. After each round, panel members receive feedback summarizing the group’s results and adjust their answers until they reach a consensus. Among the advantages of this “forecasting tool” are the anonymity of the experts, the iterative process, controlled feedback, and stability (or response consistency) of the consensus.

The study included a pool of 122 experts living across 26 countries—all distinguished scholars from various disciplines, including psychology, sociology, philosophy, economics, and medicine. The experts were presented with 26 possible dimensions of positive mental health (together with their definitions and two representative items each), which were selected from established research. On a scale of 1 (“irrelevant”) to 4 (“essential”), they were asked to assess how important each dimension was for positive mental health. The experts needed to reach more than 75 percent agreement or disagreement on whether to retain or dismiss a given dimension. If a dimension did not reach consensus after two rounds, it was removed from the study.

After three rounds of voting, a consensus on 19 dimensions was reached. Importantly, six of those dimensions received overwhelming support with more than 90 percent agreement as either “essential” or “important” for positive mental health.

The 6 dimensions of positive mental health:

  1. Meaning and purpose
  2. Life satisfaction
  3. Self-acceptance
  4. Connection
  5. Autonomy
  6. Happiness

As the authors of the study note, these dimensions echo findings from existing models of well-being. For example, the subjective well-being framework posits the three core components of well-being to be “life satisfaction,” “frequent positive affect,” and “infrequent negative affect;” self-determination theory proposes that well-being hinges upon satisfying the core psychological needs of “autonomy,” “competence,” and “relatedness;” and the six-factor model of psychological well-being includes the components of “purpose,” “self-acceptance,” “autonomy,” “environmental mastery,” “personal growth,” and “relationships.”

The experts raised a number of challenges in conceptualizing well-being.

A driver or an outcome?

When asked to determine whether each dimension was a driver or an outcome of positive mental health, the experts found it difficult to distinguish, given how closely the two are intertwined. The authors bring the example of “autonomy.” A sense of autonomy can contribute to happiness (making it a driver), which can, in turn, increase the person’s life satisfaction, which then can feed back into autonomy (making it an outcome). Nevertheless, the most commonly identified outcomes of positive mental health were the dimensions of “happiness” and “life satisfaction,” while the dimensions most often seen as drivers were “sense of safety” and “autonomy.”

Well-being is multifaceted

Source: ylanite_nietjuhart/pixabay

Well-being is inherently complex, which makes it challenging to study. Despite various taxonomies suggested over the years, distilling the concept into clear and distinct categories has proven difficult. For example, a recent large-scale study with participants from 29 countries found that 11 well-being indicators, such as “purpose in life” and “personal growth,” belonged to multiple clusters. The authors concluded that the various domains of this multidimensional construct have “fuzzy boundaries” with overlapping components.

WEIRD cultural bias

The experts pointed out the dominant WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialized, rich, Democratic) bias in psychological research, which extends to well-being studies as well. To arrive at a more comprehensive and inclusive understanding of human flourishing, it is important to incorporate diverse cultural and linguistic perspectives into all emerging frameworks of well-being. For instance, the experts raised the possibility of including dimensions from non-Western cultures, such as the Japanese ikigai (i.e., a reason for waking up in the morning).

Finally, based on the recommendations from the experts, the authors of the study reached the following definition of positive mental health:

“Positive mental health is a personal and subjective experience, where we are content with our lives, feel good, function well, and view ourselves favourably. Our level of positive mental health can vary over time, and is influenced by the way we adapt to the problems and opportunities we face. It’s impacted by many factors such as our environment, life experiences, cultural background, biology, and behaviours. Many people have some level of positive mental health, and we can improve it by taking action using a variety of means, even when we experience a mental health condition.”

As research progresses, more nuanced maps of well-being will undoubtedly emerge. In the meantime, perhaps we can take these dimensions as valuable signposts to guide our attention and effort toward living healthier, happier lives.

item.title: I Hate Myself for Using Amazon, How About You?
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

I Hate Myself for Using Amazon, How About You?

Personal Perspective: Do I betray my own values by forgoing local and unique?

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Breaking-up with a retail company can feel like ending a personal relationship.
  • The mirage of easiness can disguise problems; just because it's easy doesn't make it beneficial.
  • If you had to pay cash for a purchase, would you be as willing to pay or would you think twice?
  • Would your self-respect improve if you shopped less or made better retail purchases?

What should I do about Amazon?

I'm thinking about breaking up with Amazon the way I once thought about breaking up with a bad boyfriend. I am filled with shame because the toughest parts of ending the relationship are, in fact, the most trivial.

It comes down to convenience: A guy I dated in high school would pick me up and take me home because I didn’t drive. Amazon delivery is pretty much the same thing. They'd both do something for me and I for them; it was transactional, and nobody pretended otherwise. Available 24/7, they’d apologize if they made mistakes.

Is my self-loathing worth it when you know it’s just wrong?

I know using Amazon undermines my commitment to doing what's right by my local community. I know this the way I know I should get my fiber from eating leafy vegetables and not swallowing Metamucil, that I should remove the cellophane from a tissue box to recycle it, and that I should schedule time for weight-bearing exercises daily. I do none of those things despite knowing they are the right things to do.

The Impact on Consumer Loyalty

Amazon has worked hard to make me loyal, and I have bought into their tactics, literally and figuratively. I'm not alone. By 2024, "more than 50 percent (180 million) (of US consumers) were Amazon Prime (subscription service) members,” according to a 2025 journal paper titled “Measuring Risks Inherent to Our Digital Economies Using Amazon Purchase Histories From US," which goes on to argue that, in a revelation that's particularly stress-producing, how "easily consumers' personal attributes, such as health and lifestyle information, gender, age, and race, can be inferred from purchases."

According to Capital One Shopping, "During Prime Day alone, Amazon Prime members spent $24.1 billion" and "Amazon revenue from Prime memberships totaled $44.374 billion, representing 6.96 percent of the company’s 2024 revenue ($637.959 billion)."

Not only am I supporting poor community practices, but I'm also making myself easy prey for whatever marketing practices can take further advantage of my vulnerability. I lie to myself by deferring payment; I get the dopamine hit from the pleasure of the purchase but don't feel the pain of payment because I'm not handing over cash or even digging my credit card out of a wallet. As demonstrated in a 2026 paper published in the Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, this lack of the immediate and mindful act of handing over a form of payment can lead to poor decision-making: The "subjective pain of paying operates as a functional input to economic decision-making. Our work complements recent findings from fMRI studies, which showed increased insula activation during imagined cash payments, and aligns with behavioral evidence showing that less transparent payment methods dull the self-reported pain of paying."

article continues after advertisement

After doing some homework, just as I did in high school, I asked my friends what they thought.

The passion underlying their answers surprised me.

I heard from wholehearted fans of Amazon, such as Linda Roy, admitting, “I just can’t quit you, Amazon. If I want a size 6 adult capybara onesie, you have it. I’ll be wearing it tomorrow.”

Ray L’Heureux explains that “living in Hawaii, Prime is essential for the shipping alone; inventory is limited on the island and shipping from the mainland is cost-prohibitive.”

Ava Biffer made an undeniable point: “For some of us—a larger number than most realize, accept, or care to consider—there aren't always other choices.” Activist humorist Robin Tyler, age 84, says, “The fact is that people are now used to Amazon. It is like the invasion of AI. It’s here, I’m queer, and I accept it.”

Benefits to Authors and Workers

For some folks I respect deeply, Amazon is just fine for what it is. Historical novelist Brenda Murphy emphasized that “Amazon has almost single-handedly wrested absolute control of the publishing landscape from five multinational corporations and made it possible for a host of independently published writers to be heard. Despite their sometimes scurrilous labor policies, they do provide jobs for 1.5 million people, most of whom don't have a degree.”

“I've come to terms with my self-loathing,” shrugs humorist and writer Amy Hartl Sherman. “Amazon provides a service. I do hate that Bezos and many billionaires do not pay their share in taxes. I'm conflicted, but compartmentalized.” I believe "conflicted and compartmentalized" should be either the name of a band, or a new diagnosis, or a reality TV dating show.

Amazon Has Its Place

Small business owner Kim Robinson also believes that Amazon has a place, which is as the “retail equivalent of McDonald's. Convenient, quick, cheap, but it leaves you with a sense of dread, knowing that you have contributed to the downfall of society.”

The most unshakeable impressions, however, come from people who have chosen Amazon abstinence for moral, ethical, and political reasons.

Former student and veteran Sherry Louise was adamant: "I educated myself into a corner and realized my use of Amazon is indefensible; I refuse to be the tree voting for the axe with my dollars."

"Americans always defaulting to the easiest, most convenient, cheapest goods is part of the problem we are in right now," says physician Gary Simonds. Software developer and civic advocate Mark Spieglan referred to a word coined by Cory Doctorow describing the inexorable decline from initially consumer-friendly services into exploitative snares, driven increasingly and entirely by quick profits: "Forgive me if you're acquainted with the concept, but Amazon is the prime (pun intended) example of 'ensh*ttification.'"

article continues after advertisement

Just as I broke up with the guy in high school because it was better to face bad weather than face another round of my own disparaging self-talk, I am severing my close ties with Amazon. If I need an adult capybara onesie (size 10), I'll find one locally. Or wait until the need for one passes, realizing I'm doing fine with the onesies I've got. Amazon doesn't need me, and I hope to discover that I don't need them.
